Jahangirnagar University admission 2026–27: Applications open, 1,848 seats available
item.description:
Applications for admission to the first-year undergraduate (honours) programmes at Jahangirnagar University (JU) for the 2026–27 academic year opened today, Sunday (22 November 2026).

Prospective students can apply online from 10:00 am. The application process will remain open until 11:59 pm on 15 December.

A total of 1,848 students will be admitted to Jahangirnagar University across 37 departments and institutes this year. Interested candidates must apply online in accordance with the guidelines published on the university’s admission website.

Admission test marks and grading system

According to the admission circular published on 16 November 2026, the university has lowered the GPA requirements for all units this year. The admission test will carry a total of 90 marks, with 40 as the pass mark.

The test will comprise 80 questions carrying a total of 90 marks, while another 10 marks will be determined by candidates’ SSC and HSC results. Each question will carry 1.125 marks, up from one mark previously. The negative marking will be 0.20.

HC suspends admission tests at all public universities until 31 December

Increase in seats

The university admitted students to 1,842 seats in the previous academic year. This year, it will admit students to 1,848 seats, an increase of just six. In 2025, the number of seats increased by 10.

Application fees

Applicants must pay the application fee online using a debit card, credit card or mobile financial service. The application fee for each of Units A, B, C and D is Tk 800.

The fee for Unit E, Unit C-1 and IBA-JU has been set at Tk 600 each. A service charge of 1.2 per cent will be added to the application fee. This charge applies to all units.

Eligibility criteria for applications

*Students who passed the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) or equivalent examinations in 2023 or 2024, and the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) or equivalent examinations in 2025 or 2026, are eligible to apply.

The minimum academic requirements for the SSC or equivalent and HSC or equivalent examinations (including the fourth subject) are as follows:

Dhaka University admission: 5 steps to complete the application

Unit A (Faculty of Mathematical and Physical Sciences and Institute of Information Technology)

To apply for Unit A, which covers the Faculty of Mathematical and Physical Sciences and the Institute of Information Technology (IIT), candidates must have a combined GPA of at least 7.50 in their SSC and HSC examinations, including the fourth subject.

They must also have a minimum GPA of 3.50 in each examination separately.

In the previous academic year, the requirement for applying to this unit was a combined GPA of 8.50, with a minimum GPA of 4.00 in each examination.

Unit B (Faculty of Social Sciences and Faculty of Law)

For Unit B, candidates from the science group must have a combined GPA of at least 7.50 in their SSC and HSC examinations, with a minimum GPA of 3.50 in each.

Candidates from the humanities, business studies and other groups must have a combined GPA of at least 6.50, with a minimum GPA of 3.00 in each examination.

Unit C (Faculty of Arts and Humanities and Institute of Comparative Literature and Culture)

For Unit C, which covers the Faculty of Arts and Humanities and the Institute of Comparative Literature and Culture, candidates from the science, business studies and other groups must have a combined GPA of at least 7.50, with a minimum GPA of 3.50 in each examination.

For candidates from the humanities group, the requirement is a combined GPA of 6.50, with a minimum GPA of 3.00 in each examination.

Unit C1 (Faculty of Arts and Humanities: Department of Theatre and Performance Studies and Department of Fine Arts)

Candidates must have a combined GPA of at least 6.50 in their SSC and HSC examinations, with a minimum GPA of 3.00 in each.

Unit D (Faculty of Biological Sciences)

Candidates must have a combined GPA of at least 8.00, with a minimum GPA of 3.50 in each examination.

BUET delays admission test by 2 weeks

Unit E (Faculty of Business Studies)

For Unit E, which covers the Faculty of Business Studies, candidates from the science group must have a combined GPA of at least 7.50, with a minimum GPA of 3.50 in each examination.

Candidates from the business studies, humanities and other groups must have a combined GPA of at least 6.50, with a minimum GPA of 3.00 in each examination.

Institute of Business Administration (IBA-JU)

Candidates from the science group must have a combined GPA of at least 7.50, with a minimum GPA of 3.50 in each examination.

Candidates from the business studies, humanities and other groups must have a combined GPA of at least 6.50, with a minimum GPA of 3.00 in each examination.

How to apply

Students must first visit Jahangirnagar University’s admission website and enter the required information to check whether they meet the minimum eligibility criteria.

item.title: Chinese vloggers' videos put Uttara's Tekpara in spotlight, but settlement remains unchanged
item.description:
A canal runs along the western edge of Sector 12 in Uttara, Dhaka. On one side are a planned residential neighbourhood, wide roads and rows of high-rise buildings. On the other are narrow alleys, tin-roofed houses and a densely populated settlement. The two sides look like two different worlds. Locally, this settlement is known as Tekpara.

Tekpara has recently come into the spotlight because of live videos recorded by Chinese nationals. For months, they have roamed the settlement's narrow alleys, filming their surroundings. They have recorded videos at tea stalls, along roadsides and even inside people's homes. In some of these videos, Tekpara has been presented as New Delhi, the capital of India. Questions have also been raised about the accuracy of information shared in these videos.

On 10 November, India's Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reacted to the videos, calling for action against the Chinese nationals.

At a press conference, Jaiswal said, "It is unfortunate for both countries when people living in one country run down another country in this manner. Those involved in creating and promoting false narratives should understand that this also damages the credibility of their own country."

Although the videos by Chinese nationals have brought Tekpara into the spotlight, the settlement has a history of its own. How did a densely populated neighbourhood emerge in an area once surrounded by farmland and wetlands? Why has Tekpara remained deprived of basic civic amenities even as Uttara developed into a planned residential area? Who lives here, and how do they make a living?

Tekpara in videos, described as New Delhi

For several months, several groups of Chinese nationals have been visiting Tekpara and neighbouring areas in Uttara to record videos. Some have introduced Tekpara as New Delhi, the capital of India. They have also made derogatory remarks about the area's environment, people's lifestyles and food.

However, not all videos recorded by Chinese nationals have contained negative comments about Bangladesh. Some have also been heard making positive remarks about the country.

Local residents allege that the vloggers often enter their homes without permission while recording videos. This has caused irritation and anger among residents.

On 6 November, Prothom Alo published a report titled, Chinese citizens making live videos from morning till night, even going inside people’s homes.

Since 7 November, the Chinese nationals have no longer been seen livestreaming in different parts of Uttara. Local residents said they had not noticed Chinese nationals moving around the neighbourhood for several days.

Police at the local police station, meanwhile, said surveillance and law enforcement activities had been stepped up following media reports. Their activities have declined since then.

From elevated land to Tekpara

Tekpara is located at the northern edge of Uttara, within the jurisdiction of Turag Police Station.

Speaking to local residents, it was learnt that the area was largely agricultural land until before 2000. Rice, jute and various other crops were cultivated there. Compared with the surrounding low-lying areas, a section of what is now Tekpara stood slightly higher. Locals referred to this elevated land as 'tek'. The name of the neighbourhood gradually evolved into Fulbaria Tekpara.

Chinese vloggers no longer seen in Uttara, what were they doing?

According to residents, there were only five or six houses in the area around 1990. The rest of the land was used for cultivation. People also earned their livelihoods by fishing in the canal in front of the settlement.

One of the earliest homesteads belonged to Sheikh Nazimuddin, who died several years ago. His 55-year-old grandson Amir Hossain told Prothom Alo, "Our land was higher than the surrounding areas. That is why many people called it 'tek'. Eventually, the place came to be known as Tekpara."

Recalling the area's past, Amir Hossain said that although the surrounding areas were submerged during the 1988 floods, their homes remained above water because the land was elevated.

He remembers seeing rice and jute fields in the area during his childhood. Later, different companies began buying land and constructing buildings.

The canal was once teeming with fish

The canal in front of Tekpara also looked very different in the past. Its water was not as dirty and foul-smelling as it is today. Different types of boats used to ply the waterway, and many local residents earned their livelihoods by fishing.

Bedon Mia, 65, a local resident, told Prothom Alo that the canal water was once very clean. People made a living by catching fish. Steamers and launches used to travel along the river. Rice fields stretched as far as the eye could see on both sides. During the monsoon, surrounding agricultural land would be submerged, turning into large water bodies where local people caught fish.

Bedon Mia also described how land prices have increased over the years. According to him, a katha of land in Tekpara cost around Tk 100,000 in 2000. The price has now risen to Tk 8–9 million. In the planned residential areas of Uttara, however, a katha of land can cost between Tk 20 million and Tk 30 million.

More than 300 families, most of them tenants

While only a handful of families lived in Tekpara in the past, the settlement is now home to more than 300 families. Most are tenants. Many landowners in the area live in different affluent neighbourhoods of Uttara.

During a visit to Tekpara on 21 November, this correspondent found a densely populated settlement along a small canal. Most houses have tin walls and roofs, while some are semi-pucca structures. The internal roads are narrow and unpaved. Some areas are damp, and rubbish is scattered around the houses. There is also a noticeable lack of adequate drainage and hygienic sanitation facilities. The canal in front of the settlement emits a foul smell.

A large proportion of the residents have moved to Dhaka from different districts in search of work. Some drive auto-rickshaws, while others run small shops. Many women work as domestic helpers in nearby homes. They have settled here because rents are relatively low.

Idris Ali, a tenant in the area, told Prothom Alo that house rents are lower here than in neighbouring areas, which is why he lives in Tekpara with his family.

He moved to Dhaka with his family around 2017 because they had no land in their village. He has lived in Tekpara ever since and now works as a rickshaw puller.

Planned Uttara, an old settlement next door

Tekpara was not the only area that once had vast stretches of open fields, wetlands and low-lying land. Much of Uttara was once similar, with agricultural activities and fishing in the wetlands.

Later, to ease Dhaka's housing shortage and reduce pressure on the city, the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) took an initiative to develop a planned satellite town in the northern part of the capital.

In 2002, a research paper by Mamun Rashid, then an assistant professor at the Department of Architecture of Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), was published on the university's website under a training programme of Sweden's Lund University.

The study, titled Housing at Uttara Model Town in Dhaka City, outlines the history of Uttara's planned urban development.

According to the study, a feasibility survey for planned urbanisation of the area was conducted in June 1965. The project was initially named 'North Satellite Township'. Its name was changed to Uttara Residential Model Town in 1980.

In 1987, the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (RAJUK) was established, replacing the Dhaka Improvement Trust.

The first phase of development in Uttara was completed in 1992. Around 6,000 plots were allocated on 950 acres of land during this phase.

Development of the second phase began in 1992. It was completed in 1998, with 5,315 plots allocated on 438 acres of land.

A study titled Communities in a Growing Megacity: A Pathway to Urban Sustainability for Uttara, Dhaka, presented at the International Green Architecture Conference in 2018, provides details of the third phase of Uttara's development plan.

According to the study, planning for this phase began in 1999–2000. The project was approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) in May 2000. Land acquisition began in 2000–2001, while development work started in 2004.

The implementation of different phases of Uttara's residential projects gradually transformed the surrounding areas as well. Planned residential neighbourhoods, high-rise buildings and commercial establishments replaced agricultural land and wetlands. Land prices rose, and people's lifestyles changed.

Despite being adjacent to Uttara's planned residential areas, Tekpara continues to lag behind in terms of civic amenities. However, Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) has said it has plans to develop the area.

SM Shafiqul Rahman, chief town planner (additional charge) of DNCC, told Prothom Alo that a development plan has already been undertaken for Uttara's extended or adjoining areas, including Tekpara, Fulbaria and Nalbhog.

Residential projects developed in different phases have transformed Uttara and its surrounding neighbourhoods. Agricultural land and wetlands have given way to high-rise buildings, roads have been widened, and land prices have increased several times over.

But Tekpara remains outside this transformation. Although only a canal separates the two neighbourhoods, the gap in living conditions is considerable. Narrow alleys, tin-roofed houses and a lack of basic civic amenities remain part of everyday life in this settlement, right next to a planned urban area.

item.title: Class-I admission (2027): Apply on 1 Dec, digital lottery 15 Dec
item.description:
The applications for admission into Class-I for the 2027 academic year in all private schools and colleges across the country will commence on 1 December.

The application window will remain open until 10 December. Students for Class-I will be selected via online digital lottery at 11:00 am on 15 December.

The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) issued directives regarding this on 19 November. The guidelines signed by the Director (Secondary) of the Directorate, detailed the admission process across secondary, lower secondary and attached primary levels in private schools and school and colleges nationwide including those in Dhaka city.

According to the directives, applications for Class-I admission will be accepted exclusively online at http://gsa.teletalk.com.bd.

The application fee is set at Taka 110 which must be paid via SMS using a Teletalk prepaid mobile connection.

Applicants may select up to five schools in order of preference, subject to availability. If an applicant chooses both shifts of an institution that operates on a double-shift basis, each shift will count as one of the five choices. It will not be possible to select the same school or shift more than once.

Meanwhile, admissions for classes-II through IX must be conducted through written examinations, managed by the respective institution’s own admission committee.

In this process, the 2027 admission policy for private schools and colleges must be followed. Furthermore, instructions have been provided to ensure adherence to various quotas and catchment area requirements.

The directives also stated that the heads of institutions must publish an admission notice specifying the number of vacant seats available at their institutions.

The notice must clearly state the date and time for the submission of application forms.

The DSHE has confirmed that the selection of students for Class-I will be conducted through an online digital lottery. The admission process must be conducted under the constant guidance and supervision of the Admission Oversight and Monitoring Committee.

At the same time, transparency and accountability must be ensured throughout the entire admission process.

Detailed guidelines regarding the completion of admission applications and other admission-related procedures can be found in the ‘Secondary Circular/Order’ section of the DSHE website (www.dshe.gov.bd), as well as on the Teletalk website (www.teletalk.com.bd).

All relevant educational institutions have been instructed to carry out the admission process in accordance with the admission policy prescribed by the Ministry of Education.

item.title: Scars left in Narail's Bendarchar village
item.description:
In Kalia upazila of Narail, houses and shops belonging to several leaders and activists, including BM Kabirul Haque Mukti, a former MP of the activities-banned Awami League, have been attacked, vandalised, looted and set on fire following the murder of two leaders of the Krishak Dal and Jatiyatabadi Samajik Sangskritik Sangstha (JASAS), associate organisations of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).

This incident took place last Friday from the afternoon until midnight in the village of Bendarchar. When firefighters arrived at the scene, they saw 20 to 30 houses on fire.

Besides this, houses of three former MPs of the Awami League were also attacked and vandalised in Patuakhali. These incidents occurred between 10:00 pm on Thursday and 9:00 pm on Friday.

Meanwhile, repeated clashes broke out between BNP and Awami League leaders and activists in Bera Municipality of Pabna on Friday.

Vandalism and fire in Kalia

Earlier on Wednesday, two people were killed in an attack on a BNP motorcycle rally by activists of the Awami League in Kalia Upazila. They were Sohail Rana, general secretary of the Kalia Upazila Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Samajik Sangskritik Sangstha (JASAS), and Shahinur Islam, general secretary of the Municipal Krishak Dal.

Victims from Bendarchar village claim that on Friday afternoon, people from the BNP suddenly attacked the houses of the Awami League leaders, including Kabirul Haque Mukti and former municipal mayor Mushfiqur Rahman.

At that time, around 50 houses and shops in Bendarchar village were vandalised, looted, and set on fire. Additionally, a similar attack occurred at the house of Krishnapada Ghosh, the general secretary of the Upazila Awami League, in the greater Kalia area.

However, the local BNP denied the allegations of attacking and setting fire to any houses. Kalia Upazila BNP's General Secretary SM Wahiduzzaman told reporters that the allegations of house attacks and arson are completely baseless. The notion that these were done in the presence of BNP leaders is fictional.

Saturday, Kalia Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md Jinnatul Islam told Prothom Alo that before dusk on Friday, several houses, including that of the former MP, and 15-20 rooms were vandalised.

Five to six rooms were set on fire. They have been able to confirm attacks on the houses of former MP BM Kabirul Haque and Upazila Awami League General Secretary Krishnapada Ghosh. However, there were no casualties. The administration is not sure who carried out the attacks, but the matter is being investigated.

Police statement on the attacks

Meanwhile, a press release from the Narail District Police stated that the circulating reports of attacks, vandalism, and looting on Hindu homes in Bendarchar village are false and fabricated.

The previously recorded or AI-generated videos published by the Awami League activists on social media are misrepresenting the government and the country's image both domestically and internationally.

The press release states that there is no Hindu settlement in the Bendarchar area. No attack on any Hindu family or their businesses took place.

In response to the allegations of attacks on Hindu settlements, Kalia Upazila BNP General Secretary Wahiduzzaman said that in the last national elections, 90 per cent of the Hindu community here voted for the BNP. The Hindu community is with the BNP, and they are with them.

He further stated, "I saw on Facebook that over 200 homes were attacked; this is completely false."

The police press release noted that due to the murder of two BNP leaders, enraged relatives of the deceased and others gathered in Bendarchar village around 4: 45 pm on Friday.

They attacked the houses of several Awami League activists involved in the murder and left. The police from Kalia police station arrived at the scene and brought the situation under control. The situation is now normal, and additional police have been deployed there, the release mentioned.

Narail Superintendent of Police (SP) Mohammad Al Mamun Shikdar told Prothom Alo on Saturday afternoon over the phone that relatives and supporters of the two deceased BNP leaders attacked and vandalised three to four houses in the village. The area is not Hindu-dominated. The way it is being portrayed is not how it actually is.

Fire service statement on the arson

Kalia Upazila Fire Service Station Officer Humayun Kabir told reporters that the fire started around 4:00 pm on Friday. Due to obstacles and lack of security, they could not reach there immediately. They arrived at the scene around 8:00 pm.

While many houses were burning at the time, the fires were not very intense. They extinguished some fires while others went out on their own. There were fires in 20 to 30 houses, each having three to four rooms, so the actual number could be higher.

On-site at Bendarchar village

Saturday, around 10:30 am, this reporter visited Bendarchar village. Upon entering the village, a woman was seen leaving the area with some belongings in a pedal van, accompanied by a small child.

On condition of anonymity, she said, “There were three cows, they took them. There is not a single item left in the house. TVs and refrigerators, 10 blankets, all the things in two trunks, nothing is left in the three rooms. There's not even a quilt to cover ourselves. They destroyed the motor from the tube well.” She also alleges that her sister-in-law was threatened with rape.

Another woman named Mukta Khanom stated, “The incident happened after the Friday prayer. Around 400 people came. They vandalised and filled vehicles with whatever was there. These were all locals from Kalia, BNP people. They did the same throughout Bendarchar.”

Apart from the elderly, no other men were seen at home in the village. Many women were seen leaving their homes to go elsewhere.

item.title: Mahi wears khadi sari in Miss Universe, celebrates motherhood and motherland
item.description:
The 75th Miss Universe competition is underway in Puerto Rico in the Caribbean, with actress Samira Khan Mahi representing Bangladesh. She took to the stage for the national costume round at 5am Bangladesh time on 22 November.

Mahi’s national costume, designed around the theme of motherhood, had been revealed the day before. Wearing a red and white sari, a traditional outfit closely associated with Bengali women, she walked onto the stage with confidence, presenting a glimpse of Bangladesh through her attire.

A story of motherhood woven into Cumilla khadi

Mahi’s sari was made from Cumilla khadi fabric and designed by designer Bishwajit Mazumder. Bishwajit and his team also created the circular artwork worn on Mahi’s back, inspired by the theme of motherhood.

Bishwajit said, “We had very little time to design the sari. I had only three days. I spent the first two days developing the theme and creating the circular artwork celebrating motherhood, which Mahi carried on her back today. The sari itself was made in just one day.”

The international stage of Miss Universe offers an opportunity to showcase a country's culture and identity. Bishwajit said he chose to highlight motherhood with that in mind.

He said people also refer to their homeland as their mother, so he sought to connect the idea of mother and motherland. The circular artwork on Mahi’s back depicted a woman’s journey from childhood to becoming a mother and in the final stage of her life, finding refuge in her daughter’s embrace. Through the artwork, he sought to portray a story of affection and love passed down through generations.

Bishwajit said the sari was made from 16 yards of cotton khadi. To ensure Mahi could walk comfortably on stage and wear it with ease, the sari was pre-stitched into a ready-to-wear outfit. The border featured embroidered water lilies in a traditional kolka motif, while the sari also incorporated block-print designs.

Traditional jewellery inspired by Bengali mothers

Mahi paired the sari with gold-toned jewellery. Although gold jewellery is traditionally worn across much of South Asia, her collection drew particular inspiration from traditional Bengali ornaments.

The jewellery was designed by Tanwy Kabir, owner and designer of jewellery brand Canvas. She, too, had only seven days to complete the collection. During that time, nine artisans collectively spent 880 working hours crafting the pieces.

Tanwy said, “The traditional ornaments worn by mothers in our region in the past — Sita haar, kantha haar, bala and kantana jhumka — inspired this collection through their familiar designs, elegance and emotional significance. Through each piece, I wanted to revisit our roots, heritage and the emotions intertwined with the adornment of our mothers.”

Each piece was handcrafted by artisans with meticulous attention to detail. Beyond preserving the tradition of Bengali jewellery, Tanwy said she also wanted to showcase the skills, artistic sensibilities and craftsmanship of local artisans through the collection.

Mithila arrives in Puerto Rico with the national costume

As Mahi was selected Miss Universe Bangladesh 2026 at the last moment, she could not take her national costume with her. Her friend and Miss Universe Bangladesh 2025 Tanjia Zaman Mithila took charge of preparing the costume and accessories.

Speaking from Puerto Rico, Mahi said, “Mithila apa thought of the national costume, just as she did with everything else. Having a friend and elder sister like her meant I could manage and organise so much despite having so little time.”

Mithila arrived in Puerto Rico a day before the national costume round, carrying the outfit with her. All the elements of the costume were made in Bangladesh. To make it easier to transport, the circular artwork on Mahi’s back was constructed in nine separate pieces. The artwork depicting motherhood was made using wood, foam, fabric and shola.

Combining indigenous khadi, water lily motifs, traditional jewellery and the story of motherhood, Mahi’s national costume brought together Bangladesh’s culture, craftsmanship and emotional heritage in a single presentation.
