item.title: Nearly 8 in 10 women suffer from anaemia, study finds
item.description:
Poor nutrition, excessive menstrual bleeding, child marriage and early motherhood are leaving women increasingly vulnerable to anaemia. The problem is further compounded by a deeply rooted tendency among many women to put their families' nutritional and healthcare needs ahead of their own, often at the cost of their health.
As a result, women are almost twice as likely as men to suffer from anaemia, according to a recent study.
Conducted among adults seeking healthcare at four rural unions in the Chittagong division, the study found that 77.9% of female participants were anaemic, compared with 39.7% of their male counterparts.
Published in the international journal Health Science Reports on October 10, the study found that 59.3% of the 459 participants were suffering from anaemia.
Of those affected, 27% had mild anaemia, 29.6% had moderate anaemia and 2.6% had severe anaemia. This means nearly half of the anaemic participants were suffering from moderate to severe forms of the condition.
The gender gap was particularly pronounced in moderate anaemia. Women were 2.51 times more likely than men to have mild anaemia and 11.53 times more likely to have moderate anaemia. Although women also faced a higher risk of severe anaemia, the small number of cases made the estimate less certain.
The study also found that underweight individuals were 3.42 times more likely to develop moderate anaemia than those with normal body weight.
Researchers initially considered data from 2,118 adults seeking healthcare at four rural unions. However, the final analysis included only 459 participants with available haemoglobin test results, comprising 235 women and 224 men.
The researchers stressed that gender-based differences in anaemia risk should be considered when developing prevention and treatment strategies for rural communities.
Women's vulnerability to anaemia stems not only from nutritional deficiencies but also from increased nutritional demands at different stages of life and inadequate health awareness.
Excessive menstrual bleeding, pregnancy and childbirth increase the body's demand for iron and other essential nutrients. However, many women fail to consume enough nutritious food to meet these requirements, increasing their risk of anaemia.
Public health specialist Dr Mahbuba Jamil told Dhaka Tribune that malnutrition, child marriage and early motherhood were among the major contributors to anaemia among women in Bangladesh.
She said early marriage and pregnancy increase the body's nutritional requirements, but many women do not receive sufficient iron and other essential nutrients through their diets, leaving them vulnerable to anaemia.
A lack of awareness about nutrition further aggravates the problem, she said, adding that understanding the nutritional value of different foods and planning diets accordingly could help prevent the condition.
Dr Mahbuba stressed that nutritious food does not necessarily mean expensive fruits or costly food items. Alongside fish, meat and eggs, locally available vegetables and foods such as papaya and bananas can also provide essential nutrients.
Growing vegetables in home gardens or other available spaces can also help families meet their nutritional needs, she added. Urging women to pay equal attention to their own diets, she said many families prioritise nutritious food for children, husbands and other members while women themselves often neglect their dietary needs.
"This tendency must change," she said.
However, Dr Mahbuba cautioned against treating the study's findings as representative of women across the country, noting that anaemia rates may vary between regions.
She said chronic diseases, infections and genetic factors could also cause anaemia, making it important to identify the underlying cause in each case.
Unequal food distribution within families and women's tendency to neglect their own health are also significant contributors to the problem.
Renowned medicine specialist Professor Dr ABM Abdullah said rural women, in particular, often lack awareness about nutrition and personal healthcare. While they pay considerable attention to the dietary needs of other family members, they frequently overlook their own.
Many mothers prioritise nutritious food for their children, husbands and other family members at the expense of their own nutritional needs, he said.
He added that women often hesitate to seek medical advice even when they fall ill. During adolescence, many girls conceal menstrual health problems due to embarrassment or social stigma. Delayed treatment can eventually lead to various health complications.
Dr Abdullah also highlighted food discrimination between boys and girls within families. Even in households where both boys and girls grow up together, boys are often given better food while girls' nutritional needs are overlooked.
Such discrimination must end, he said.
According to the specialist, preventing anaemia requires greater awareness not only among women and adolescent girls but also among other family members.
Fish, meat, eggs, lentils, vegetables and other iron-rich foods should be included in regular diets. Consuming vitamin C-rich fruits alongside iron-rich foods can also improve the body's absorption of iron.
He also emphasised the need to ensure proper nutrition and reproductive healthcare for adolescent girls.
Preventing child marriage, ensuring safe motherhood and maintaining adequate intervals between pregnancies are essential, he said, explaining that sufficient time between childbirths allows mothers to recover physically and replenish their nutritional reserves.
Experts also called for regular health check-ups and access to treatment for rural women through community clinics, health workers and mobile healthcare services.
Women suffering from moderate to severe anaemia should be referred promptly to appropriate healthcare facilities for treatment.
Anaemia generally refers to a condition in which the haemoglobin level in the blood falls below the normal range. Although iron deficiency is one of its most common causes, it is not the only underlying factor.
Vitamin B12 deficiency, chronic inflammation, infections and inherited blood disorders can also cause anaemia. Certain long-term illnesses may contribute to the condition as well.
Experts caution that people should not take iron supplements without medical advice simply because they have been diagnosed with anaemia. Identifying the underlying cause is essential before beginning treatment.
Necessary tests, including haemoglobin and ferritin assessments, should be conducted, with treatment prescribed according to medical advice.
The significantly higher prevalence and severity of anaemia among women underscore the need to prioritise the nutrition, healthcare and health awareness of women and adolescent girls in public health policies and programmes.

item.title: Indian media: 4 Awami League leaders visit Petrapole to assess Hasina's return route
item.description:
Four senior leaders of the activities-banned Awami League visited the Petrapole border crossing in West Bengal on Sunday to assess a possible route for former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's return to Bangladesh, according to Indian media reports.
Indian media outlets Hindustan Times and TV9 Bangla reported the visit, while News18 had earlier reported that the delegation planned to inspect the crossing to assess whether Hasina could use it to enter Bangladesh.
The delegation reportedly held a nearly two-hour closed-door meeting in the immigration area following the visit.
The delegation comprised Awami League Presidium members Jahangir Kabir Nanak and Mofazzal Hossain Chowdhury Maya, Joint General Secretary AFM Bahauddin Nasim, and former member of parliament Alauddin Ahmed Chowdhury Nasim.
Former minister Nanak is facing trial before the International Crimes Tribunal over allegations of crimes against humanity committed in Dhaka's Mohammadpur during the July 2024 uprising. Bahauddin Nasim, meanwhile, has been sentenced to death in a separate case involving crimes against humanity during the uprising.
According to reports by Indian media, the leaders left Kolkata's New Town area at around 9am and reached Petrapole, opposite the Benapole border crossing, at around 2pm. They departed for Kolkata at approximately 3:50pm.
The reports also said the delegation may examine alternative routes through Tripura, including the Agartala-Akhaura border crossing.
A visit to the Tripura border region is reportedly planned for Tuesday, November 24, followed by an assessment of the route connecting Maharaja Bir Bikram Airport with the Akhaura border crossing on Wednesday, November 25.
In a November 22 report, Moneycontrol said the leaders were likely to visit Petrapole to assess a possible route for Hasina's return. The outlet also noted that no official timeline or confirmed plan for her return had been announced.

item.title: Indonesia seizes 405 tons of hazardous chemical bound for Bangladesh
item.description:
The Indonesian Navy has seized 405 tons of sodium perchlorate, a powerful oxidising chemical used in industrial processes and the manufacture of certain explosives, from a Bangladesh-bound vessel in the coastal waters off Belawan, Indonesia.
The Comoros-flagged vessel, MV Star Line, was detained on November 7 while travelling from China to Bangladesh, Indonesian news outlet Waspada.id reported.
Indonesian Navy Regional Command-1 (Koarmada I) Commander Rear Admiral Denny Septiana disclosed the information at a press conference in Belawan on Friday, November 20.
He said the vessel had stopped in Belawan waters to refuel when personnel aboard the Indonesian Navy patrol vessel KRI Sigalu-857 noticed unusual movements.
The patrol team became suspicious after finding that the vessel was operating outside its designated route and contacted it for further inspection.
Subsequent checks revealed inconsistencies in the vessel's documents and cargo. The commander of KRI Sigalu, in coordination with Koarmada I headquarters, then ordered a search.
According to Denny, the vessel was carrying 36 containers, 15 of which contained sodium perchlorate, a strategic chemical used as an oxidizer. The total quantity of the chemical was 405 tons.
Authorities also found discrepancies in the vessel's registration documents. The documents listed its International Maritime Organization (IMO) number as 8356962, official number as 1902384 and call sign as D-6A4384.
Although the documents stated that they were valid until October 8, 2027, their validity status was listed as suspended.
Denny said authorities were examining the vessel's administrative documents, the validity of its navigation permits and whether it had complied with regulations governing the transportation of dangerous goods.
The Indonesian Navy said investigations and questioning were underway to identify those involved in the incident.

item.title: Study: US influence in Asia plunges as China closes gap
item.description:
The United States has lost a significant amount of power and influence in Asia this year, research has shown, with China gaining ground.
The Lowy Institute’s 2026 Asia Power Index found that the Trump administration’s war with Iran and other unpopular policy decisions had contributed to a record decline in US diplomatic influence in Asia.
China, by contrast, held steady across most measures, while strengthening its military capability, cultural influence and resilience, adding to its overall power in the region.
China ranked first in the Index’s measures of Economic Relationship and Diplomatic Influence, ahead of the US in both.
While Washington remains the dominant power in the region according to the index, the gap between the US and China’s military capabilities is now at its narrowest point on record.
“This narrowing divide owes more to Washington’s missteps than to any advances on Beijing’s part,” authors Hunter Marston and Jack Sato wrote.
“Respondents to the Asia Power Index survey saw the United States as distracted and disengaged in Asia.”
Australia’s comprehensive power score dipped slightly from last year, and it fell one place to sixth, behind Russia.
The report credited Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with advancing Australia’s economic interests but rated him less effective at furthering diplomatic interests in Asia.
The index found the Trump administration’s diversion of resources away from the Pacific to the Middle East coincided with deeper defence ties among US treaty allies in the region.
“The United States’ unresolved war with Iran has eroded US military capabilities by depleting its stockpile of long-range missiles, and profoundly undermined perceptions of US diplomatic influence both regionally and globally,” the report said.
That, along with the US pressing countries to spend more on their own defence and calling for fewer joint military exercises with South Korea, left negative impressions of US leadership, the report said.
With the US recording declines in economic and military capabilities, the two superpowers — China and the US — are now almost tied in economic capability in the region.
“The gap between the two is now 5.3 points, the narrowest since the inception of the Index, but it’s still a clear lead for the US,” said Sato, a data analyst and researcher on the Asia Power Index at the Lowy Institute.
He told the ABC that the narrowing comprehensive power scores reflected three factors.
“A series of missteps by a more transactional US”, conflicts elsewhere “drawing US attention and its defence networks away from the Indo-Pacific”, and China’s fast military expansion decreasing the US lead in Military Capability “from 27 points in 2018 to just over 15”.
“The narrowing gap reflects a decline in US power, rather than a rise in China’s,” Sato said.
It was a tough year for countries in the Asia-Pacific region, with the disruption of global energy supplies from the Middle East conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure hitting the region particularly hard.
Higher fuel and fertiliser prices constrained food and agricultural production, putting more political pressure on leaders.
As a result, government effectiveness declined across nearly all South-East Asian nations, with Singapore, Myanmar and Laos the exceptions.
Diplomatic influence also fell in nearly every country covered by the index.
Countries also struggled to navigate US tariffs, rising tensions in the South China Sea and ongoing competition between the United States and China.
Indonesia saw the greatest drop in diplomatic influence, a decline the report said largely reflected the country’s “haphazard approach to foreign policy” under President Prabowo Subianto.
In a year when most countries failed to gain diplomatic influence, India became more influential overall in Asia.
The country’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi is now considered to be the second-most effective regional leader, behind Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“For the assessment of Modi’s regional leadership, it’s largely stability at a time of upheaval,” Sato said.
“A key factor we’ve found is continuity. Both Prime Minister Modi and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar have established themselves in their roles.”
India has more political influence in the region now than when the index began eight years ago, although China’s power remains 80 per cent higher than India’s.
“India did struggle in 2026 with many internal challenges, which saw its scores for Economic Capability and Resilience decrease,” Sato said.
He also said the country’s Diplomatic Influence score dipped slightly, “but by much less than others in the region”.
“India has a very strong demographic and economic outlook, with, comfortably, the third-highest Future Resources score in the region.”

item.title: One killed, two injured in blender explosion at Hazaribagh residence
item.description:
A woman was killed and two others injured after a blender machine reportedly exploded at a second-floor apartment in Bottola, Hazaribagh, Dhaka, on Sunday evening.
The deceased was identified as Parvin. The injured were identified as Fatema Akter Urmi, 20, and Farida Begum, 60.
Farida was taken to the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery, while Urmi was taken to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH).
A doctor at the burn institute said Farida sustained cuts to different parts of her body from shattered glass but had no burn injuries. She was given initial treatment before being referred to DMCH.
Farida, who works as a cook at the apartment, said the explosion occurred while she was operating the blender.
Neighbour Rahim Islam, who helped take Farida to hospital, said he was sitting at a tea stall in front of the building when he heard a loud explosion. The apartment's windowpanes and parts of a wall were shattered.
He said he rushed to the scene and found Farida lying in a pool of blood. Several other people were also injured. With the help of locals, he rescued Farida and took her to hospital.
A Fire Service duty officer said firefighters recovered a severely mutilated body from the scene.

item.title: School should be the safest space for every learner
item.description:
A mocking laugh in class, a hurtful message forwarded online or silence when a classmate is harassed can make students afraid to return to school. Every child in Bangladesh has the right to walk through the school gate free from fear. Protecting that right takes work throughout the school year. Every secondary school should have trained staff, clear procedures to prevent violence, and respond when students report it.
Globally, about one in three students reports being bullied. Estimates put the share of children affected by cyberbullying at around one in ten . Harm can be amplified online through image-based abuse and sexual extortion. Girls and boys can face different forms of violence, and poverty and disability can increase the risks. Fear can make it harder for students to learn even when they are in class.
Bangladesh has made gains in girls’ enrolment. Today, girls are enrolling in secondary schools at higher rates than boys. Yet many leave before completing Grade 10 .
The latest 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey found that about half of women aged 20 to 24 years had married before the age of 18. In the most recent 2024 Violence Against Women Survey , about 62% of ever-married girls aged 15 to 19 years reported experiencing intimate partner violence in the preceding year. Schools and communities both have a role in addressing the pressures girls face beyond the classroom.
A situation analysis on Health Promoting Schools , published in 2026 by the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) with Unesco’s support, surveyed 458 students and 206 teachers across the country. Only 30.1% of teachers reported having received training in health education or well-being.
The study suggested that health topics receive limited classroom time partly because they are not examined. Schools can build on that support by involving families in work on safety and well-being.
The Health Promoting Schools approach makes health and well-being part of how schools teach and operate. By 2021, more than 90 countries and territories had adopted the initiative and the global Health Promoting Schools (HPS) standards and indicators published by WHO and Unesco.
Unesco’s Education for Health and Well-being strategy links healthy school systems with age-appropriate life skills and health education with learning environments free from violence and bullying. The 2023 Unesco Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development identifies the safety, health, and well-being of learners and education personnel as a guiding principle. It calls for strengthening the school system to support students’ physical and mental health.
Since 2024, DSHE and the National Academy for Educational Management (NAEM), with Unesco’s support, have been piloting HPS in 30 schools in urban and rural areas of Bangladesh. The pilot has generated evidence, adapted the standards and indicators for Bangladesh and developed a competency-based curriculum for teachers, delivered through master trainers. Alongside DSHE’s Learning Acceleration in Secondary Education (LAISE) project and its cyberbullying training, it has supported reporting through complaint boxes and school anti-sexual harassment committees.
We call on government, development partners, and communities to extend this work to every secondary school, starting where need is greatest. The Health Promoting Schools standards adapted for Bangladesh can serve as a national benchmark. Each school should have a code of conduct, a complaint box, and a committee responsible for school safety.
A complaint box gives a student a way to speak up. What happens after a report determines whether that student gets help. Schools should be able to refer students confidentially to health, psychosocial, social, and legal services.
Education, health, social welfare, and law enforcement agencies should plan together so schools know where to turn. Union parishads and upazilas can help make school surroundings safer.
Teacher training should cover the skills set out in the HPS approach, including positive discipline and digital safety. Prioritize government and rural schools, where the study found teachers had received less training.
The curriculum and textbooks should teach students how to recognize and respond to online abuse, protect their privacy, and use the internet responsibly. Parents and teachers need these skills too, so they can support children when harm occurs online.
Families, religious and community leaders, and young people have a role in changing the norms that sustain child marriage. When a girl or boy drops out, schools and communities should follow up and help that learner return.
Schools should assess safety each year, plan and carry out improvements, then monitor and review progress. They should track violence, attendance, and dropout alongside the HPS indicators and learning outcomes. Pilot schools can share what works, and the findings can inform Bangladesh’s reporting under Unesco’s 2023 Recommendation.
Bangladesh’s promise of an education for every child must be kept in the classroom, on the way to school and in the online spaces children use. When a student can speak up about harm, receive support, and return to learning in safety, that promise is being put into practice.
Professor Dr Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel , Director General, Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education. Professor Dr Wasim Md Mazbahul Haque , Director General, National Academy for Educational Management. Dr Susan Vize, Head of Office and Unesco Representative to Bangladesh.

item.title: We are losing the fight against dengue
item.description:
With 518 confirmed deaths as of writing this editorial and fast approaching 175,000 hospitalizations recorded so far this year, marking the third-deadliest outbreak in Bangladesh’s history, our response to dengue remains inadequate, to say the least.
Why such a response has descended from disappointing to outright infuriating is because three years after the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) drafted the National Dengue Prevention and Control Strategy (2024-2030), virtually zero tangible progress is visible on the ground.
Dengue has long been far more than an unpredictable seasonal anomaly and rather an annual public health emergency. Yet, the battle against dengue is one Bangladesh continues to lose because of chronic administrative incompetence.
As prominent entomologists and public health experts have rightly pointed out, the national strategy itself is fundamentally flawed, allegedly drafted behind closed doors by bureaucrats without input from entomologists or field specialists, rendering it unscientific and detached from reality.
Worse still, even the basic directives within that document remain unexecuted. Year-round destruction of Aedes breeding grounds is nonexistent, coordination between the health ministry and local government bodies remains broken, and disease surveillance misses countless cases treated or lost at home.
Equally inexcusable is the continued centralization of treatment. By failing to equip district and upazila hospitals with adequate diagnostic kits, skilled personnel, and intensive care capacity, authorities force critically ill patients from across the country to undertake perilous journeys to Dhaka, overwhelming capital hospitals.
Bureaucratic inertia continues costing innocent citizens their lives. If the government wants to demonstrate that it truly cares about people’s suffering, then it must immediately overhaul its failed approach. We cannot keep treating preventable deaths as inevitable statistics.

item.title: Constable stabbed to death while gathering intelligence in Narayanganj
item.description:
A police constable was stabbed to death while collecting intelligence in plain clothes in Fatullah, Narayanganj, on Sunday night.
The incident took place around 10:30pm in the Hashembag area of Kashipur Union. The deceased, Anwar Hossain, 32, was posted at the Shitalakkhya Police Outpost under Narayanganj Sadar Model Police Station.
Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime) Tarek Al Mehedi said an assistant sub-inspector (ASI) and Constable Anwar came under attack by several people while gathering intelligence in plain clothes.
Anwar died after being stabbed with a sharp weapon, he said.
The ASI, Abdus Sattar, who was accompanying Anwar, managed to escape by fleeing the scene. His physical condition was not immediately known. Police are trying to identify those involved in the attack, Tarek said.
He added that the Hashembag area has several drug hotspots, where law enforcement agencies have previously conducted raids, seized drugs and arrested suspected drug dealers.
Investigators are examining whether a drug trafficking syndicate was behind the attack, he added.

The injured were identified as Nayan, 24, Jony, 18, Nirab, 24, Nayan, 26, Robin, 25, and Palash, 40.

item.title: Ex-MP Nixon named prime accused in Krishak Dal leader murder case
item.description:
A murder case has been filed against former MP Mujibur Rahman Chowdhury Nixon, naming him as the prime accused, along with 95 others, over the killing of Raju Mollah, joint organising secretary of the Bhanga upazila unit of Jatiyatabadi Krishak Dal in Faridpur.
Another 100 to 150 unidentified people have also been accused in the case.
Raju's wife, Ria Begum, filed the case with Bhanga Police Station around midnight on Saturday.
Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Mizanur Rahman confirmed the matter around 10pm on Sunday. Raju was the son of Akhtar Mollah of Bakpura village in Nurullaganj Union under Bhanga upazila. He also served as joint organising secretary of the upazila unit of Krishak Dal.
On November 17, Raju was critically injured in an attack allegedly carried out by leaders and activists of the activities-banned Awami League near Hamirdi bus stand in Hamirdi Union at around 9:15pm. He was taken to Bhanga Upazila Health Complex, where the attending doctor declared him dead.
Nixon, a former MP from the Faridpur-4 constituency comprising Bhanga, Sadarpur and Charbhadrasan, was named accused No 1 in the case filed on Saturday night. His 95 followers were also named in the FIR.
According to the FIR, the other accused blocked a highway near Hamirdi bus stand on Nixon's instructions and with his financial backing. They allegedly lit torches and placed brick chips, stones and bamboo sticks on the road.
They were also carrying locally made weapons, including spears, machetes, cleavers and crude bombs, the FIR stated.
At around 7:45pm, the accused intercepted Raju while he was riding his motorcycle. Accused No 2, Shahadat Khoyrati, 41, of Hazarahati area in Bhanga municipality, allegedly stabbed him on the right side of his waist with a sharp spear, leaving him seriously injured.
The FIR further alleged that several other accused, including Al Amin, 45; Asibur Rahman Farhan, 42, former general secretary of the banned Jubo League's Bhanga municipal unit; Ashikuzzaman, 36, convener of the banned Chhatra League's Bhanga upazila unit; Bala Mia, 46; Kamal, 45; and Belayet Munsi, 38, beat Raju.
At one stage, they allegedly dragged him along the road, scraping the skin from the right side of his abdomen to his right knee and leaving him bloodied.
A police team led by Bhanga OC Mizanur Rahman and Sub-Inspector Khalid Mahmud reached the scene around 8:15pm after receiving information about the incident.
The accused allegedly hurled brick chips and stones at the police and snatched a walkie-talkie from SI Khalid Mahmud. Police later brought the situation under control.
Raju was rescued from the scene and taken to Bhanga Upazila Health Complex around 9pm, where the attending doctor declared him dead.

item.title: Police informant shot at shop in Chittagong
item.description:
A police informant was shot and critically injured by 3 armed men at his furniture shop in Fatikchhari upazila of Chittagong around 7pm on Sunday.
The incident took place at the shop in the Dighirpar area, north of Kanchannagar Temuhani Bazar. The victim, Md Abchar, 40, is the son of Mohammad Sahabu Chowdhury of the same area.
According to police and eyewitnesses, 3 armed men arrived on motorcycles and fired 4 rounds at Abchar while he was sitting at his shop before fleeing the scene.
Local residents rescued him in critical condition and took him to Nazirhat Upazila Health Complex. As his condition deteriorated, the attending doctor referred him to Chittagong Medical College Hospital (CMCH) for better treatment. He remains in critical condition.
Fatikchhari police station Officer-in-Charge Robiul Alam Khan told Dhaka Tribune that the attackers fired 2 rounds from a shotgun and 2 rounds from a 9mm pistol.
"One bullet hit Abchar in the thigh and 2 bullets hit his hand. Besides, pellets from the gunfire also injured his chest," he said.
The officer-in-charge added that Abchar used to support the police and suggested that this might have been a motive behind the attack.
Assistant Police Superintendent of Hathazari Circle Kazi Md Tarek Aziz said Abchar was receiving treatment at CMCH Hospital.
"Those who carried out this incident will be identified and brought under the law," he said.

item.title: Execution is everything for development projects
item.description:
The 16 recent development projects approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) worth Tk33,298.48 crore, of which less than Tk500cr will be from external sources, is certainly an ambitious push to strengthen rural connectivity, revive dying waterways, and bolster agricultural productivity.
From constructing 256 long rural bridges to excavating nearly 8,900 kilometres of canals, small rivers, and waterbodies across 444 upazilas, we can admire the scope and scale of these initiatives and can recognize that they target genuine developmental needs.
Building pillar-free bridges that protect natural river flows while linking remote communities, alongside restoring surface water irrigation across 2.65 lakh hectares of farmland, could deliver lasting economic and ecological dividends. These are interventions that are necessary for future prosperity.
With that said, Bangladesh’s development landscape is full of well-intentioned infrastructure schemes ruined by bad planning and worse implementation as a result of corrupt practices.
At a moment when public finances are stretched razor-thin amid severe revenue shortfalls, high inflation, and mounting debt obligations, every single taka is precious. As such, we have zero margin for waste, vanity spending, or bureaucratic lethargy.
Equally important is ensuring full safety before the project is greenlit for the implementation stage. To that end, that there remain dozens of bridges which still have not undergone feasibility studies does not inspire confidence, and must be addressed promptly. Approving massive construction packages before completing rigorous hydrological surveys and engineering assessments is a recipe for disaster.
If these projects are to succeed, the government must enforce ironclad fiscal and operational discipline from day one. Beyond ensuring the bridges requiring feasibility studies undergo thorough, independent technical evaluations, strict timelines and fixed budget ceilings must be enforced, along with penalties for contractors and project directors who manufacture artificial delays to inflate costs.
Approving projects has always merely been the starting line. It is disciplined, corruption-free execution that has eluded us.

item.title: Why cancel culture will never stick in Bangladesh
item.description:
Walk past any cha-er dokan in Dhaka on a humid evening and you will witness the true theatre of Bangladeshi public opinion.
One week, the table is united in righteous fury over a global brand, a viral clip, or a celebrity’s court-premises clash.
Voices rise, thumbs fly across cracked screens, and solemn pledges of permanent ostracization are made.
Two weeks later, the exact same crowd is arguing about cricket selections, inflation, or the next three-second clip to cross their feeds, reaching without a second thought for whatever they had just sworn off.
Cancel culture -- that distinctly Western export built on moral registries, algorithmic pile-ons, and long-memoried corporate or career exile -- never quite survives the journey to Bangladesh.
Not because Bangladeshis lack passion. Quite the opposite: We have passion in industrial quantities.
The problem is our attention span, our social fabric, and a deeply ingrained cultural habit of moving on before the kettle has even stopped whistling.
The anatomy of a thirty-day boycott
Consider the wave of consumer anger directed at Coca-Cola in Bangladesh following the escalation of the Gaza war and the backlash over its local advertising missteps.
For a stretch, boycotting multinational brands felt like a moral badge worn across timelines, with local alternatives like Mojo and RC Cola enjoying a visible surge of patriotic goodwill.
Yet retail realities in Bangladesh are notoriously stubborn.
Convenience, price points, distribution muscle, and sheer habit have a way of eroding ideological resolutions once the peak of a news cycle passes.
Even when a campaign dents sales or forces a PR scramble, turning a burst of moral indignation into permanent market erasure requires sustained discipline -- something mass outrage rarely maintains once life’s daily pressures resume.
The same short half-life shows up in celebrity and media flashpoints. Take the recurring storm around actress Pori Moni and her volatile clashes with journalists -- from heated exchanges and allegations of phone-snatching around court appearances to live-streamed accusations of "terrorism in the name of journalism."
Journalists’ associations have called protests or boycotts, commentators have dissected every angle, and social media has briefly crowned winners and villains.
Yet in Bangladesh’s entertainment and tabloid ecosystem, outrage and publicity are often Siamese twins.
A figure who is "cancelled" in one clip can re-emerge in another viral moment days later, carried forward by the very curiosity that fuelled the condemnation.
From 1990s print panics to 2020s timeline storms
Fickleness is not a gift bestowed solely on smartphones; it is an old habit wearing new clothes.
In the 1990s, as private newspapers, FM radio, and satellite television began opening up Bangladesh’s media landscape, public panics and moral outrages already moved in brisk cycles -- whether around sensational crime coverage, shifting political slogans, or cultural debates over foreign television and music.
Back then, distance and slower print cycles meant a controversy had to work harder to travel, and once the next edition hit the stands, yesterday’s scandal was already losing oxygen.
By the 2010s and 2020s, Facebook and short-form video turned that slow burn into instant wildfire.
Over the last decade and a half, Bangladesh has seen countless online storms: Sudden boycotts of specific TV dramas or advertisers, fierce pile-ons against influencers and public figures, and rapid shifts in what the entire nation is "definitely not watching or buying anymore."
History has shown that social media in Bangladesh can power massive real-world mobilization when grievances run deep and structural -- as seen during the student-led anti-discrimination uprising -- but ordinary cultural "cancelling" rarely holds.
Most online boycotts here behave less like court sentences and more like monsoon rain: Loud, dramatic, impossible to ignore for an hour, and quickly soaked into the pavement.
Across borders and back home
Zoom out across South Asia and the wider world, and you see why this pattern looks so familiar. Across South Asia, Bollywood and regional film industries have repeatedly faced hashtag boycotts -- sometimes hurting an opening weekend or two, only for audiences to return whenever a film’s buzz or star power hits the right chord.
In the West, where cancel culture is often treated as an inescapable social guillotine, even high-profile cancellations frequently turn out to be porous: Audiences split, algorithms move on to fresh targets, and figures with loyal niches often claw back visibility or reinvent themselves.
If cancel culture struggles to stay rigid even in societies built around individualist branding and HR-style accountability, it stands even less chance in Bangladesh.
Western cancel culture thrives on a tidy moral ledger: You cross a line, the crowd withdraws its patronage, and institutions enforce the exile.
Bangladesh does not run on tidy ledgers.
Our social life is dense, relational, and forgiving in ways that are both generous and frustrating.
Personal ties, addas , kinship networks, political alignments, and economic survival constantly cut across neat moral lines.
What looks like an unbreakable boycott on a Monday morning often dissolves into pragmatism -- or plain boredom -- by Friday afternoon.
Why we never quite stay mad
There is also a quieter truth behind our fickle-mindedness: Living in Bangladesh already demands a high daily quota of outrage.
Between traffic, rising living costs, workplace stress, and constant political or civic noise, nobody has the emotional bandwidth to stay furious at a soda brand or an actress’s press-scrum temper forever.
None of this means public criticism in Bangladesh is pointless.
Calling out bad ads, holding public figures accountable, or questioning corporate behaviour matters when it sparks real debate.
But expecting a Western-style cancel culture to permanently erase people or products in Bangladesh is misreading the room.
Here, the crowd rarely holds a grudge long enough to finish the sentence -- because by then, another notification has already lit up the screen.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Can Bangladesh turn its hard-won progress into lasting strength?
item.description:
Over the past four decades, Bangladesh has undergone a substantial economic transformation. From a predominantly agrarian economy marked by widespread poverty, the nation has built a robust manufacturing and export infrastructure, significantly increased remittance inflows, and improved key human development indicators. Notably, the ready-made garment (RMG) sector has emerged as a significant player on the global stage.
However, economic resilience goes beyond endurance during adverse conditions; it reflects an economy's capacity to absorb shocks, recover quickly, and adapt effectively while safeguarding the welfare of its populace. For Bangladesh, this paradigm has become increasingly critical as it confronts a range of challenges, including persistent inflation, financial-sector vulnerabilities, insufficient investment, climate change-related risks, geopolitical volatility, and the complex imperative of advancing beyond its current status as a least-developed country (LDC).
Again, while Bangladesh is classified as a least developed country, academic discourse offers different views on whether the government of Bangladesh should keep or change its status. The biggest LDC benefits for Bangladesh have been:
Bangladesh's status as an LDC has facilitated export-led growth, particularly in the RMG sector, but has also led to a reliance on external trade benefits. This dependency poses challenges, as Bangladesh must move beyond preferential treatment and focus on productivity, innovation, and diversification.
To maintain its global standing as a productive, independent economy, Bangladesh must strengthen competitiveness. Consequently, Bangladesh should analyze its LDC graduation with a focus on socio-economic and political factors to build a sustainable competitive framework post-graduation.
The World Bank indicates that the immediate economic forecast for Bangladesh is still uncertain, with GDP growth anticipated to be 3.9% for FY2026. This prediction comes amid persistent inflation, rising poverty, and significant pressure on the banking sector, requiring strategic action to strengthen economic stability and support continued growth.
The nation averaged about 6% annual GDP growth over the last decade. As the country's largest export-driven sector, the RMG industry is crucial but vulnerable because it relies heavily on a single industry. According to the World Trade Organization, garments make up about 81% to 84% of Bangladesh's merchandise exports, ranking the sector among the most vital sources of foreign currency and jobs in the country. More than half of the roughly 4.5 million workers in this sector are women.
Remittances also serve as an essential safety net. Bangladeshis employed abroad remit billions of dollars home each year, supporting household spending and foreign-exchange availability. These trends suggest Bangladesh's resilience does not rely on a single institution or policy; instead, it has developed through a mix of export manufacturing, overseas employment, agriculture, local entrepreneurship, women’s workforce participation, and a robust domestic market.

Bangladesh's export achievements have been modest, but reliance on a single sector adds risk. The garment sector accounts for most merchandise exports, with primary markets in the European Union and the United States. According to the WTO, about 40% of Bangladesh’s garment exports went to the EU and 18% to the US in 2024.
This focus makes Bangladesh vulnerable to fluctuations in global consumer trends, trade regulations, supply chains, labour standards, and environmental expectations. The country's anticipated transition from least-developed-country (LDC) status signifies a significant challenge.
While graduation is a noteworthy achievement, some trade benefits linked to LDC status will eventually change. The WTO highlights that the Bangladeshi business community is particularly worried about sustaining market access and complying with stricter rules of origin.
Thus, for Bangladesh, building economic resilience increasingly means shifting from low-cost competitiveness to improving productivity, quality, technology, and skills, and diversifying exports.
Bangladesh's economy has become increasingly vulnerable to global political and economic disturbances because it relies on imported energy, export markets, remittances, global supply chains, and foreign currency. The World Bank stresses the urgent need for policy reforms to reestablish macroeconomic stability, boost revenue collection, fortify the financial sector, and improve the business climate to encourage job creation and inclusive growth. Many low-income workers continue to struggle with stagnant wages that erode their purchasing power.
While external pressures eased in FY25 and early FY26 due to strong remittance flows and a more adaptable exchange rate, financial sector vulnerabilities remain elevated, with a non-performing loan ratio of over 30%. Small and medium-sized enterprises face considerable challenges, including high regulatory costs and inadequate infrastructure, underscoring the need for targeted deregulation and stronger competition policies to promote private sector development.
In Bangladesh, the primary focus tends to be on real GDP growth rather than the future dollar value of GDP. Variations are significant because different institutions use different forecast dates, assumptions, and models.
The IMF's January 2026 forecast estimated growth of 4.7% for both FY2026 and FY2027, but its July 2026 staff assessment later revised FY2027 growth to 3.5%, showing how forecasts can shift as conditions change.
The ADB's September 2026 outlook maintained its growth projection for Bangladesh at 3.7% for FY2026. The World Bank's most recent country outlook for Bangladesh projects growth of 3.9% in FY2026, rising gradually to 5.3% by FY2028.
Another dimension Bangladesh cannot afford to overlook is climate change.
Bangladesh is highly exposed to floods, cyclones, river erosion, salinity, and other climate-related hazards. These are not merely environmental problems. They can destroy infrastructure, reduce agricultural production, displace workers, and increase government expenditure.
The IMF has identified building resilience to natural disasters as a major priority for Bangladesh and has called for climate-resilient infrastructure and greater access to climate finance.
This makes Bangladesh an important example of why economic resilience and climate resilience are increasingly inseparable.
Perhaps the most important question is not simply whether Bangladesh's GDP can recover. It is who benefits from recovery.
A resilient economy should protect vulnerable households while creating opportunities for workers, entrepreneurs and young people. Recent data indicate that Bangladesh has faced declining labour-force participation, with women disproportionately affected.
The World Bank reported that labour-force participation fell from 60.9% to 58.9% between 2023 and 2024, while women accounted for 2.4 million of the additional three million working-age people outside the labour force.
This suggests that resilience needs to include employment resilience.
Bangladesh's large young population can be a demographic advantage if workers receive appropriate education, digital skills, technical training, and access to productive employment. Conversely, insufficient job creation could turn demographic potential into economic pressure.
Small and medium-sized enterprises also deserve particular attention. The World Bank notes that many SMEs face regulatory costs, unreliable infrastructure and limited access to finance.
A resilient Bangladesh cannot depend exclusively on large garment exporters. It needs a broader ecosystem of competitive firms across manufacturing, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, information technology, logistics, tourism, financial services and other knowledge-intensive sectors.
The economic history of Bangladesh offers a crucial insight: Resilience does not mean dodging every crisis. Every economy faces challenges. Instead, resilience requires the institutions, capabilities, and social frameworks needed to endure disruptions and come back stronger.
Despite exploitation discourse, Bangladesh has already proven its ability to adapt and evolve in the garment industry; increased overseas employment, rising remittances, and advances in the agricultural sector, with minimal human development, show that adaptation is achievable.
Corruption, political instability, and lack of social justice can seriously obstruct Bangladesh's ability to convert economic growth into widespread, sustainable advancement. Corruption can misappropriate public funds, undermine institutions, deter investment, and diminish the efficiency of public services. Political instability and uncertainty can disrupt policy-making, erode investor confidence, and delay essential economic and institutional reforms.
Additionally, a lack of social justice -- evidenced by unequal access to education, healthcare, job opportunities, and legal protections -- can marginalize disadvantaged groups and exacerbate social inequality. Together, these issues can erode public trust and institutional effectiveness, constraining Bangladesh’s ability to turn its economic potential into inclusive development and higher living standards.
The World Bank warns that without structural changes in revenue generation, the financial sector, and the business environment, Bangladesh's previous resilience could wane. The IMF supports this view, saying reforms are crucial to restore macroeconomic stability and promote long-term development.
For Bangladesh, the key economic challenge is transformation. It is no longer simply about rapid growth; it now involves building an economy that can sustain prosperity amid evolving global trade dynamics, worsening climate challenges, technological shifts in employment, and the declining reliability of traditional competitive strengths.
The country's next development phase may depend on its ability to shift resilience from merely enduring shocks to consistently adapting and creating new opportunities.
This transition would redefine economic resilience not merely as a response to crises, but as a core component of Bangladesh's long-term growth strategy.
Dr ASM Anam Ullah (PhD) is an Australian senior academic, editor, human rights activist, political and economic analyst, and OHS and industrial relations expert.
